newsitem.title: GERMANY: Fall in German jobless echoes forecasts - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Fall in German jobless echoes forecasts - analysts.

text.p: News that German unemployment in March is likely to show an unadjusted decline of 190,000 from February's 64-year record of 4.67 million was greeted by economists as a positive development on Monday, but they said it was largely in line with expectations.
After seasonal adjustment, such a decline would translate into a fall of 15,000 to 25,000, said economist Holger Fahrinkrug at UBS in Frankfurt.
Sources with access to Federal Labour Office data told Reuters the number of unemployed declined in both western and eastern Germany. The official data are due to be released on Tuesday.
"Any decline is good, but this is largely in line with the consensus," Fahrinkrug said.
Gernot Nerb at Salomon Brothers agreed. "The normal change for the time of year would have been a fall of 170,000, so this is a seasonally adjusted fall of around 20,000.
"But this is a relatively modest improvement, and the new jobs will have come almost exclusively from the construction sector," Nerb said.
"People are being hired back into the building sector, but not as fast as they were laid off. We can expect this effect to fade over the next few months."

Nerb said it remained open to question whether the government would be able to realise its target of cutting unemployment to an average 4.2 million this year, a figure that underpins its budget plan to help Germany meet the Maastricht treaty deficit goal of three percent of GDP.
Forecasts by 10 economists polled earlier by Reuters showed expectations of a seasonal decline of up to 85,000, to flat at the other end. Most foresaw a decline of about 50,000.
Fahrinkrug said, "After two distorted months it is hard to gauge the underlying trend, but I think we have passed the trough in the labour market."
He added, however, that he did not expect major jobs growth this year.

With Germany straining to bring its budget deficit down to three percent of GDP to qualify for the single European currency, Fahrinkrug said he expects the effort to fall short of the mark, hampered by high unemployment among other factors.
Still, he expects Germany to be among the starting line-up for EMU, even if its deficit is 3.1 or 3.2 percent of GDP.
"It will be very hard to push through cuts social in social spending this year, he said.
